justice: The street provides basic pedestrian space on both sides and marked zebra crossings at the intersection, showing some distribution of space beyond cars.
However, the carriageway is extremely wide compared with the visible sidewalks, so road space is still allocated primarily to motor traffic rather than balanced among all users.
No dedicated bicycle lane or protected cycling space is visible, which weakens equity for cyclists.
Accessibility appears only moderate because curb ramps, tactile paving, and other barrier-free details are not clearly visible at the crossing edges.
The open intersection geometry and central refuge island help crossing legibility, but the long crossing distance can still disadvantage slower or mobility-limited users.
safety: Marked zebra crossings are visible on multiple legs of the intersection, which gives pedestrians a designated crossing path.
The roadway is very wide and open, encouraging higher vehicle speeds and increasing exposure time for people crossing.
A narrow median/refuge island with signage offers some separation and may provide a partial waiting area in the middle of the crossing.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, which supports nighttime visibility and basic traffic safety.
No protected bike lane, bollards, or strong traffic-calming elements are visible, so cyclists and pedestrians remain relatively exposed in this large intersection.
livability: The street edge has very limited visible active frontage, with only sparse buildings and large open roadside land, so everyday street life appears weak.
There are almost no visible pedestrians, cyclists, outdoor seating areas, or commercial amenities that would indicate social vitality.
Some trees line the roadside and median edges, adding a minimal landscape element, but they do not create a lively or service-rich public realm.
The intersection feels more like an auto-oriented corridor than a neighborhood place for lingering or social interaction.
Large vacant-looking plots and low building density reduce the sense of convenience and daily-use urban activity.
sustainability: Rows of roadside trees provide some ecological value and limited green infrastructure compared with a fully paved corridor.
The very large paved road surface suggests high land consumption and heat absorption, which lowers environmental performance.
No visible bus stop, transit shelter, or dedicated cycling facility is present to strongly support low-carbon travel choices.
The open planted strips and undeveloped roadside land may allow some stormwater infiltration, but no explicit bioswale or rain-garden infrastructure is visible.
The corridor's design appears strongly oriented toward motor vehicles, which weakens sustainability despite the presence of street trees.
aesthetics: The road appears clean, orderly, and well maintained, with clear pavement markings and relatively neat edges.
Evenly spaced streetlights and regularly planted trees create a simple, consistent visual rhythm along the avenue.
The broad sky view and uncluttered corridor give the scene a spacious character.
At the same time, the very wide asphalt surface dominates the view and makes the streetscape feel monotonous.
Sparse buildings and limited facade detail reduce visual richness and place identity.
comfort: Thermal comfort is limited because the road is extremely wide and exposed, while tree canopy coverage is too sparse to shade most walking or cycling areas.
Physical comfort is only moderate because the pavement looks smooth for vehicles, but no benches, shelters, or resting facilities are visible for people outside cars.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the low traffic volume and open sightlines reduce immediate conflict, but the oversized intersection can feel exposed for pedestrians and cyclists.
Streetlights and clear markings improve orientation, which slightly supports user confidence in the space.
The small amount of greenery softens the environment somewhat, but not enough to offset the harshness of the expansive asphalt.
walkability: Zebra crossings are present, so formal pedestrian crossing opportunities do exist at the intersection.
The crossing distance is very long because of the unusually wide roadway, which reduces convenience and increases pedestrian effort.
Sidewalks are visible at the edges, but they appear secondary relative to the road and lack strong enclosure, amenities, or shade.
No benches, shelters, shopfronts, or active destinations are visible along the street, reducing walking attractiveness.
The median refuge island offers slight help for crossing, but overall the corridor remains weakly pedestrian-oriented.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, painted cycle track, or physically protected cycling space is visible anywhere in the scene.
The intersection is very wide, so cyclists would need to mix with turning and through motor traffic across a large paved area.
There is no visible bicycle parking, bicycle signal, or bike-specific wayfinding to support convenient cycling.
The road surface appears smooth and the traffic volume looks low at this moment, which offers a small benefit for confident cyclists.
Overall, the street geometry and allocation of space clearly prioritize motor vehicles over bicycles.
